strengths: Addresses a practically important and under-studied question: whether pretraining hyperparameters optimized for validation loss also optimize downstream (post-fine-tuning) performance, bridging pretraining and post-training literatures.

Extensive experimental design spanning two model families (Llama-2, OLMo-2), multiple scales (up to 4B), two training regimes (20 TPP and 140 TPP compute-optimal/overtrained), six diverse fine-tuning tasks, and six evaluation metrics covering both correctness and quality.

The paper is appropriately cautious about the strength of its correlational claims; e.g., it explicitly runs a leave-one-out stability analysis (Fig. 3/9) showing that the pretraining-loss-vs-downstream-performance correlation is unstable, rather than overselling a fragile correlation.

The mechanistic investigation (linear probing for representation separability, attention matrix pseudo-rank, train-val gap for overfitting) provides a multi-pronged, theoretically grounded (e.g., connecting to Kobayashi et al. 2024's nuclear-norm argument, Jacot et al. 2024's neural collapse) attempt to explain the observed plasticity effect, going beyond a purely empirical correlation.
Thorough appendix documentation of hyperparameters, datasets, and additional per-task/per-metric results, aiding reproducibility.

The core empirical finding (higher-than-default weight decay improves downstream fine-tuning performance) is reasonably consistent across the many settings tested, which is a nontrivial and potentially impactful result for pretraining practice.
weaknesses: Weight decay sweeps are very sparse for the larger/more expensive configurations: Llama-2-4B-20x is tested at only two values (0.1 and 1.0), and OLMo-2-1B-140x at only three values (0.1, 0.3, 1.0). Claims about the 'optimal' weight decay for these settings are therefore weakly supported—the reported optimum may simply be the better of very few options tested, not a true optimum.

No mention of multiple seeds or repeated fine-tuning/pretraining runs; given that several test sets are small (e.g., PubMedQA n=1000, MMLUProCoT n=567) and some reported downstream accuracy differences are modest, the absence of variance estimates or significance testing makes it hard to assess how much of the observed trend is signal versus noise.

The three proposed mechanisms (linear separability, attention rank reduction, reduced train-val overfitting gap) are established as being correlated with weight decay and, in one case, correlated with downstream performance (Fig. 15), but no causal or interventional evidence (e.g., directly manipulating rank or separability independent of weight decay) is provided to confirm these are actually the drivers of plasticity rather than co-occurring epiphenomena.

Model scale is modest (up to 4B parameters, trained on relatively small token budgets); it remains unclear whether the findings generalize to the much larger models and dataset scales used in modern frontier LLM pretraining, which the paper's motivation section explicitly targets.

The range of weight decay values differs inconsistently across model setups (e.g., Llama models tested up to 10.0, OLMo models only up to 1.0), which complicates direct cross-family comparisons and obscures whether the identified 'optimal' values are truly comparable across settings.

Fine-tuning hyperparameters (e.g., whether weight decay is also used during SFT, and its value) are not clearly discussed, leaving open a potential confound between pretraining weight decay effects and fine-tuning regularization.

For the 140 TPP regime, the paper notes the optimal weight decay for downstream performance (0.3) is lower than for 20 TPP (1.0) but higher than the pretraining-loss-optimal value (0.1), yet the very sparse grid (3 points) prevents confident characterization of this trend, and extrapolation to longer training in the discussion is speculative.

strengths: Comprehensive and systematic empirical study spanning two model families (Llama-2, OLMo-2), multiple scales (0.5B-4B), two training regimes (20 TPP and 140 TPP compute-optimal/overtrained), and a wide array of 12 downstream tasks (CoT reasoning, language understanding, safety alignment) with multiple correctness/quality metrics (Greedy, Maj@16, Pass@16, RM@16, ORM, Correct Ratio).

Addresses an important and underexplored question: whether pretraining hyperparameters selected to minimize validation loss also optimize downstream (post-trained) performance. The demonstration that higher weight decay can simultaneously worsen pretraining loss and improve downstream performance is a genuinely useful and practically relevant finding for the field.

Strong robustness checks: additional sweeps jointly varying pretraining learning rate and weight decay, and fine-tuning learning rate/weight decay/batch size, consistently show the same qualitative effect, which increases confidence in the core finding beyond a single hyperparameter configuration.

Multi-pronged mechanistic investigation (linear probing for representation separability, attention matrix rank analysis building on and extending Kobayashi et al., and train-val loss gap analysis) provides plausible, converging explanations for why weight decay aids plasticity, going beyond a purely correlational headline result.

Transparent and detailed reporting: extensive appendices with hyperparameter tables, per-task figures, stability analysis of correlation coefficients (leave-one-out), and an explicit, honest limitations section that acknowledges the correlational nature of the mechanistic claims and the small sample sizes for some model groups.
weaknesses: The three proposed mechanistic explanations (linear separability, low-rank attention, reduced overfitting) are explicitly acknowledged as correlational rather than causal; no intervention experiments (e.g., directly manipulating attention rank or probing accuracy while holding weight decay fixed) are performed to disentangle these mechanisms from confounding effects of weight decay itself.

Sample sizes for the largest/most compute-intensive settings (Llama-2-4B-20x: 3 weight decay values; OLMo-2-1B-140x: 4 values) are quite small, limiting the granularity and statistical confidence of the optimal weight decay estimates in exactly the regimes (larger models, longer training) most relevant to frontier LLM practice.

All models studied (≤4B parameters, ≤210B tokens) are far smaller than modern frontier pretraining runs; the paper itself notes uncertainty about whether the optimal weight decay trend continues to decrease beyond 140 TPP, so extrapolation to very large-scale, heavily overtrained frontier models (where the practical stakes are highest) remains unverified.

The operationalized notion of "plasticity" (downstream accuracy after SFT) conflates classical plasticity (retained capacity to fit new data) with transfer/generalization quality, and it is not fully disentangled from other benefits weight decay might confer during fine-tuning itself (e.g., interacting with the FT optimizer) versus purely a property of the pretrained checkpoint.

The study only considers supervised fine-tuning as the post-training paradigm, omitting RLHF/RL-based post-training, which is increasingly central to modern LLM development pipelines and may exhibit different plasticity dynamics.

Correlation analyses between pretraining loss and downstream performance are based on small per-group sample sizes (n≤10) and are shown by the authors' own leave-one-out stability analysis (Figure 10) to be quite unstable in sign and magnitude, somewhat weakening the strength of the quantitative (though not qualitative) claims in Section 4.3.
